nodes.label: In the US, no legal status, wants to stay
Enroll in a school that sponsors F-1 students
nodes.chip: a school has to agree to sponsor you
nodes.gate: The school must be certified to sponsor international students. Most community colleges are not. You need a real degree, not a certificate mill — the government audits for exactly that.

nodes.label: F-1 student status
nodes.gate: The school files the SEVIS I-901 for you and requests the status change; you do not file alone.

waits.note: The I-901 fee is paid by the school; the I-539 is filed with USCIS.

nodes.label: Co-op or internship (CPT)
nodes.gate: Curricular practical training: work tied directly to your coursework, no extension, and no route to a green card. Useful while studying, useless afterwards.

nodes.label: Optional Practical Training (OPT)
nodes.gate: Requires one full academic year, or two if your English was not your native language.

waits.note: You get at most 12 months, and 90 days of unemployment.

nodes.label: 24-month STEM OPT extension
nodes.gate: Requires a degree in a STEM field on the eligible list.

waits.note: Adds 24 months. The longest runway a student gets.

nodes.label: H-1B cap registration
nodes.gate: Registration is a lottery, once a year, and not everyone who registers is picked. Being picked only buys you time in the country — it is not a green card. If you are already inside the US, the odds you were not picked in an earlier round are the odds you face now.

nodes.label: Get a job offer from a willing employer
nodes.gate: The employer has to agree to sponsor you, and to stay with you. Most employers will not. Sponsorship attaches to the job, so you cannot freely switch employers the way a citizen can.

waits.note: Premium processing is a large extra fee and only buys speed, not eligibility.

nodes.label: L-1 intracompany transferee
nodes.gate: Requires you to have worked for the parent company abroad for a full year in the last three. It is cap-exempt: you do not have to win the H-1B cap lottery the way an H-1B applicant does.

nodes.label: O-1 extraordinary ability
nodes.gate: A high bar: sustained acclaim, awards, publications, or recognition. Not a category most people qualify for, and the file is expensive to build.

nodes.label: Choose an immigrant category (EB-1 to EB-5)
nodes.chip: the categories are numbered by how little you are worth
nodes.gate: Five categories, ordered by what the government thinks your labour is worth. EB-1 is extraordinary ability, EB-5 is a $800,000 investment. Where you land decides how long you wait.

nodes.label: PERM labor certification
nodes.gate: The employer must run a recruitment process first: pick a wage level, post the ad, wait out the 30 and 60 day minimums, sift resumes. Months of employer admin before the government even looks at it.

waits.regular: over a year, often considerably more
waits.note: A Department of Labor form, not a USCIS one. Audit reviews take substantially longer than analyst reviews. Not eligible for premium processing.

nodes.label: Immigrant petition for an alien worker
nodes.gate: This is the step that sets your priority date. Everything you wait afterwards is counted from the day this is filed, not from the day you get the card.

waits.note: 45 business days for EB-1C and EB-2 National Interest Waiver under premium processing.

nodes.label: Wait in the visa-bulletin queue
nodes.gate: This is a different queue from the one USCIS is processing you in, and it is the one that turns into a decade. It is also the one that can move backwards when the government publishes an update.

waits.backlogs: China and India far longer — Indian EB-2 dates date from 2013
China and India far longer — Indian EB-3 dates date from 2013

waits.note: The government is not granting these at all right now.

waits.backlogs: Longer for Chinese and Indian investors, since 2014 and 2019 respectively

nodes.label: Adjustment of status to permanent residence

waits.note: You can only file once your priority date is current. This wait is separate from the queue above and does not include it.

nodes.label: A relative files for you
nodes.gate: A US citizen or a green card holder has to petition for you. Someone with no qualifying relative in the US has no family path at all — this is the single largest fork in the whole system.

waits.note: The same form, roughly three times the wait, because the sponsor is waiting their own turn to become a citizen.

nodes.label: Immediate relative — no queue
nodes.gate: Spouse, parent, or unmarried child under 21 of a US citizen. This is the only kind of applicant who never waits in the visa bulletin. Everyone on every other path is behind someone.

waits.bulletin: no wait — exempt from the bulletin
waits.note: The bulletin wait and the processing wait are shown separately on purpose; only one of them applies here.

nodes.label: Family preference category — you are in line
nodes.gate: Everyone who is not an immediate relative is in a numbered preference category, and the number decides which queue you are in.

waits.category: F2A — spouses of green card holders
F2B — adult children of green card holders

waits.bulletin: roughly 18 years, and far longer for some countries
waits.backlogs: Indian siblings date from 2006, Mexican from 2001, Philippine from 2008
waits.note: The longest ordinary wait in the system.

nodes.label: Adjustment of status to permanent residence

waits.note: Filed only once the bulletin date is current. This wait does not include the queue.

nodes.label: Fiancé(e) of a US citizen
nodes.gate: This petition is only half of it. The visa interview at a US consulate abroad is the other half, and that part is not shown on this page because we do not have reliable figures for it.

waits.note: USCIS approval only. Consular processing follows.

nodes.label: Apply for asylum
nodes.gate: You must apply within a year of arriving, or within 180 days if you are already in removal proceedings. Missing that deadline is usually fatal to the claim.

waits.note: Timing depends entirely on the adjudication schedule, and an approved grant is not a green card — it is protection plus work permission.

nodes.label: Temporary Protected Status
nodes.chip: temporary — not a path to a card
nodes.gate: Only if your country of origin is currently designated, and you have been continuously present in the US since the designation. The designation is reviewed every year and can end.

waits.note: TPS is not a route to permanent residence. It defers the question; it does not answer it.

nodes.label: U visa — crime victim
nodes.gate: Requires cooperation with law enforcement in a qualifying crime investigation. After four years you can adjust to permanent residence.

waits.note: A path to a green card, unlike TPS and DACA.

nodes.label: DACA
nodes.chip: temporary — not a path to a card
nodes.gate: Arrived in the US before 16, under 31 today, in school or graduated, and no felony conviction on record. Every one of those has to be true at once.

waits.note: DACA gives work permission. It does not lead to a green card.
